title: Training patterns associated with injury in New York City Marathon runners
authors: Toresdahl BG, Metzl JD, Kinderknecht J, McElheny K, de Mille P, Quijano B, Fontana MA
population: 735 New York City Marathon registrants (mean age 41.0, 46.0% female) monitored for 16 weeks with Strava
findings: 49,195 training runs tracked; injury during training 40.0% (294/735), during or right after the marathon 16.0% (112/699); illness during training 27.2% (200/735).
Runners first injured in training quarter 3 ran less in quarter 2 than uninjured runners (27.7 vs 31.9 miles/week, p=0.018).
Runners first injured in quarter 1 had more days with 7-day to 28-day distance ratio (ACWR) >=1.5 (injured IQR 0-3 vs uninjured 0-1 days, p=0.009).

Multivariable logistic regression: each day with ACWR >=1.5 was associated with training injury (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.02-1.10, p=0.002). Thresholds of 1.3 and 1.5 were analysed, but the abstract reports results for 1.5 only.
limitations: Self-reported injury at 4-week intervals; distance-only ACWR with known statistical criticisms; per-day OR is small; registrants are a motivated sample; association, not proof that ratio caused injury.
implications: Use a soft guard: avoid weeks where last-7-day distance is 1.5 or more times the 28-day distance; the 1.3 level is a D-grade early-warning default, since no result at 1.3 is in the abstract.
The lower mileage in the preceding block among later-injured runners is a single secondary comparison; do not treat it as evidence that low volume prevents injury or that high volume is safe.

verification.notes: Crossref title, journal, first author, 7 authors match; abstract re-fetched. Level lowered B to C (moderate n, small effect, ACWR criticisms). Researcher's claim about the 1.3 threshold rewritten, since abstract reports no 1.3 result.
